findings.explanation: Initially, `done` is the fourth-position callback, `name` is the second argument, and `opts` is the truthy third argument or `null`; the ordinary four-argument overload therefore retains all three. A second-position function becomes `done` and clears both the alternate name and options. Otherwise, a third-position function becomes `done`, clears options, and preserves a string filename. A second-position object is treated as options exactly when the third argument is a function or is `undefined`: it becomes `opts` and the alternate name is cleared. In the object-plus-third-callback overload, this branch runs after callback normalization, so the normalized callback remains in `done`. After deriving headers/options and `fullPath`, `download` returns `this.sendFile(fullPath, opts, done)`; it does not start a separate transfer. On an ordinary Express response this property dispatch reaches the public camel-case `res.sendFile`. The saved graph independently records the later direct call from public `sendFile` to lowercase `sendfile`; the `download` property call is dynamically dispatched rather than represented as that private-helper edge.

The attachment name is formed from `basename(name || path)`: a nonempty alternate name wins, while an empty or otherwise falsy name falls back to the original source path. This changes only the attachment naming input; `fullPath` is still computed from `path`. A fresh headers object always contains the generated `Content-Disposition`. `Object.keys(opts.headers)` copies only the supplied header object's own enumerable properties, and the lowercase comparison prevents every casing of `Content-Disposition` from replacing the generated value. The derived options object is `Object.create(opts)`, so supplied options are inherited through the prototype rather than copied. With no options, `opts` is `null`, producing a null-prototype derived object. Its fresh own `headers` property shadows any inherited headers. The wrapper does not assign into the original options or original headers object; subsequent `sendFile` assignment of `etag` also lands on this derived child. By contrast, direct `sendFile` calls use and mutate their supplied options object. Root is read through the derived object, including its prototype: a falsy or absent root causes `resolve(path)` to be passed, while a truthy root preserves the original `path`. This truthiness handoff does not itself establish filesystem containment.

The public entry point is camel-case `res.sendFile`. Missing or falsy paths—including `undefined` and the empty string—synchronously throw the required-argument `TypeError`; consequently, falsy non-strings are caught there too. A truthy non-string synchronously throws the string-type error. These two checks precede second-position callback normalization. A relative string synchronously throws later unless `opts.root` is truthy; an absolute string or a relative string with a truthy root passes this gate. All validation occurs before URI encoding, imported-stream creation, or entry into the private helper. Options default to a fresh `{}` when absent/falsy. A second-position function becomes `done` and also gets a fresh options object. Otherwise, an ordinary truthy options object is retained by identity. The path is passed through `encodeURI`, then `opts.etag` is unconditionally overwritten with the application's current `etag` setting. Thus a direct call mutates the caller's options object; a download call mutates only download's prototype-derived child. The imported `send` function is invoked as `send(req, pathname, opts)` to obtain `file`. That object, the response, and the same options reference are then handed to the distinct lexical lowercase private helper `sendfile`; it is not another invocation of the public method.

If a callback was supplied, it has unconditional precedence over default routing: every private-helper completion immediately calls `done(err)`, including success with `err` undefined, synthetic directory/abort errors, and original transfer errors. This branch performs no automatic response, `next` call, or `headersSent` check, so the callback's caller owns subsequent handling. Without a callback, `EISDIR` calls `next()` without an error. `ECONNABORTED` and errors whose `syscall` is `write` are left alone. Every other error calls `next(err)`, while successful completion does nothing further. There is no `try`/`catch` converting synchronous setup exceptions into this completion path: validation and other synchronous work before the line-406 handoff propagate to the caller and do not enter `sendfile` or invoke `done`.

Before piping, the helper registers five unconditional file listeners in order—`directory`, `end`, `error`, `file`, and `stream`—then registers response completion through `onFinished`, and finally registers the optional `headers` listener. Only after all applicable registrations does it call `file.pipe(res)`. Each helper invocation has its own `done` guard. Directory and abort handlers synthesize new errors (`EISDIR, read`/`EISDIR` and `Request aborted`/`ECONNABORTED`); the error handler forwards its original error object; and `end` completes successfully with no argument. Terminal handlers set `done` before invoking the callback, so repeated or callback-reentrant terminal events are ignored. Multiple deferred finish checks can be scheduled before completion, but the same guard lets only the first terminal outcome call back. Headers are not applied eagerly: when a `headers` event occurs, the handler reads the then-current `options.headers`, enumerates its own enumerable keys at that time, and forwards each current value to `setHeader` on the event's `res` argument. Replacing or mutating that headers object before the event therefore affects this enumeration. A failure before any headers event has caused no header writes by this listener; the code does not guarantee whether an event follows, and the listener has no `done` check if one does. Conversely, once writes occur, later terminal failure handling contains no rollback or header removal. Under the stipulated nonthrowing header operations, these writes do not themselves enter completion routing.

`streaming` starts as `undefined`; a `stream` event assigns `true`, while a `file` event assigns `false`, so whichever state event occurs most recently supplies the value observed later. When `onfinish` receives `ECONNRESET`, it routes through guarded `onaborted`, converting that condition into the helper's synthetic `ECONNABORTED` error. Any other finish error is forwarded unchanged through guarded `onerror`. If completion already occurred, those handlers—or the explicit no-error `done` check—make finish a no-op. A non-error finish is not immediate success: it schedules `setImmediate` without first marking completion. The deferred function reads the latest `streaming` and `done` values. If state is still `undefined` or is `true` and no terminal event has won, it reports an abort; only state `false` can proceed to guarded successful completion. State events occurring before the deferred function can therefore alter that result. If `end`, `directory`, `error`, an error-bearing finish, or another deferred finish completes in the interim, it sets `done`; the queued check then exits without a duplicate callback.
